---
title: "Lactate transport"
description: >-
  Blocking the transporters that carry lactate out of the cell breaks the
  metabolic dependency that fibroblasts need to drive pulmonary fibrosis.
order: 10
toc: false
---

::: {.fig-wide}
![](/img/research/ipf-trichrome.jpg){fig-alt="Trichrome-stained section of lung from a patient with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. Collagen is stained blue."}

[Lung tissue from a patient with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. Collagen is stained blue.]{.fig-note}
:::

Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis affects roughly 150,000 people in the United States,
and median survival after diagnosis is three to five years. The two approved drugs
slow the disease but do not stop it, and for advanced disease a lung transplant
remains the only option. Better targets are needed.

Fibrosis is driven by myofibroblasts — activated cells that fill the lung with
excessive scar tissue. Turning an ordinary lung fibroblast into a myofibroblast is
not only a change in behaviour; it is a change in metabolism. Myofibroblasts burn
far more glucose than resting cells, and they convert most of it to lactate.

That creates a vulnerability. A cell running glycolysis this hard has to get the
lactate out, and it does so through a family of proteins called monocarboxylate
transporters. **If lactate cannot leave, the metabolic program that supports
fibrosis cannot be sustained.**

::: {.fig-narrow}
![](/img/research/lactate-pathway.jpg){fig-alt="Diagram of glycolysis showing glucose converted to pyruvate and then to lactate, with lactate exported from the cell by monocarboxylate transporters, and the inhibitors that block each step."}

[Glycolysis, and the points in it that drugs can block. Lactate export by MCTs is the step we target.]{.fig-note}
:::

We found that two of these transporters, MCT1 and MCT4, are increased in the lungs
of patients with pulmonary fibrosis and in experimental models of the disease.
Blocking either one — genetically or with small molecules — prevents fibroblasts
from becoming myofibroblasts, in cells from healthy donors and from patients alike.
In mice, MCT inhibitors reduce lung fibrosis, and they do so in aged animals as well
as young ones, which matters because this is a disease of older people.

Blocking lactate export does not simply starve the cell. It reroutes it. Fibroblasts
treated with these drugs shift toward oxidative metabolism, produce fewer reactive
oxygen species, and stop directing glucose carbon into the scarring regions of the
lung. We are now working out how that metabolic shift is read by the cell's
machinery for switching genes on and off, and which cells in the lung the drugs must
reach in order to work.
